title: Parking Lot
summary: The canonical multi-entity LLD prompt: spot-assignment strategy, ticketing, pricing, and a concurrency wrinkle at the gate where two cars race for the last spot.

slides.markdown:
The parking lot is the LLD interview's warm-up that isn't actually easy: it looks like CRUD on a
few classes, but it's really testing scoping speed. A strong candidate has `ParkingLot`, `Level`,
`Spot`, and `Ticket` sketched and a car parking in under 10 minutes, then spends the rest of the
interview on the two things that actually differentiate a good answer: the spot-assignment
strategy and the concurrency at the gate.

Treat every requirement you can't finish as a deliberate non-goal, say so out loud, and move on.
Interviewers penalize slow scoping far more than a missing feature.

slides.sectionTitle: Requirements: levels, spot types, entry/exit, ticketing, pricing
slides.markdown:
State the shape before the classes: a lot has multiple **levels**, each level has **spots** of
different types (compact, large, motorcycle, EV, handicap), vehicles **enter** through a gate that
issues a **ticket**, and **exit** through a gate that computes a **fee** from that ticket.

Say your non-goals out loud early: payment-gateway integration (assume `processPayment(amount)`
just returns success/failure), license-plate recognition, and multi-lot routing are all reasonable
things to declare out of scope in a 45-minute round. "I'm assuming X so I can focus on Y" reads as
judgment; silently skipping X reads as an omission.

slides.sectionTitle: Core entities: ParkingLot, Level, ParkingSpot, Vehicle, Ticket, gates
slides.markdown:
The entity list mostly writes itself: `ParkingLot` owns a list of `Level`s, each `Level` owns
`ParkingSpot`s, a `Vehicle` (tagged with a `VehicleType`) occupies a `ParkingSpot`, and parking one
produces a `Ticket` linking vehicle, spot, and entry time.

The entity candidates skip: **gates**. `EntryGate` and `ExitGate` aren't just methods on
`ParkingLot` — they're physical, independently numbered hardware with their own state (open,
closed, which ticket-printer or card-reader is attached). Modeling them as classes, not calls, is
what lets you answer "what if entry gate 2 breaks" or "add a fourth entrance" without redesigning
anything else.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: class diagram for the multi-level, multi-spot-type lot
slides.markdown:
![ParkingLot aggregate with Level, ParkingSpot, and Ticket](assets/parking-lot-class-diagram.svg)

`ParkingLot` is the aggregate root: it holds the `Level`s and exposes `parkVehicle`/`unparkVehicle`
as the only entry points. Every other class — `Level`, `ParkingSpot`, `Ticket` — is reachable only
through it, which is what stops a caller from grabbing a spot without going through assignment and
ticketing.

assets.alt: ParkingLot aggregate with Level, ParkingSpot, and Ticket

slides.markdown:
"Which spot does this car get?" has more than one reasonable answer, so don't hardcode it. A
`SpotAssignmentStrategy` interface with one method, `findSpot(Level, VehicleType)`, lets you swap
**nearest-available** (minimize walk distance from the entrance), **size-matched** (a motorcycle
shouldn't take a large spot if a motorcycle spot is free), or a custom rule like reserving EV spots
for EVs only.

This is the Strategy design pattern doing real work here, not decoration: `ParkingLot` calls the
interface and never branches on a policy name, so adding a new assignment rule means adding a
class, not editing `ParkingLot`.

slides.sectionTitle: Deep-dive: allocation without a full-lot scan
slides.markdown:
A `SpotAssignmentStrategy` that scans every spot on every level to find one that's free and the
right type is O(spots) per car — fine for a toy lot, embarrassing at 5,000 spots during a rush.

The fix: each `Level` keeps a `Map<SpotType, Queue<ParkingSpot>>` of currently-free spots,
populated once at startup. "Find a free compact spot" becomes `freeSpots.get(COMPACT).poll()` — a
queue pop, not a scan. Parking removes a spot from its bucket; leaving puts it back. Lookup cost
stops depending on lot size entirely.

slides.sectionTitle: Diagram: the free-spot index — per-level, per-type buckets
slides.markdown:
![Level free-spot queues keyed by spot type](assets/parking-spot-buckets.svg)

Two operations touch this structure: `park` polls a spot out of the bucket matching the vehicle's
type, and `exit` offers the freed spot back into its bucket. Both are O(1), and this structure is
exactly what makes the next slide's concurrency fix possible — there's a single place to make
atomic.

assets.alt: Level free-spot queues keyed by spot type

slides.sectionTitle: Concurrency: two cars, one last spot
slides.markdown:
Two cars pull up to different entrances of the same level at the same instant, both see "1 compact
spot free" in the index, and both try to take it. If assignment is "search, then mark" as two
separate steps, both searches can succeed before either mark runs, and you've double-booked a spot.

The fix is making **reservation** the atomic step, not the search that precedes it. Instead of
"read the bucket, pick a spot, then mark it taken" as three operations, treat "pop a spot out of
the bucket" itself as the one atomic action — whichever car's pop runs first gets the spot, and the
second car's pop on an empty bucket correctly reports "none free," not a duplicate. This is the
same class of race you'll see in object-oriented concurrency generally: never split "check" from
"act" across two steps a second thread can interleave with.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: Level.reserveSpot(type) as an atomic pop
Pricing as its own Strategy object
slides.markdown:
Pricing changes far more often than the parking logic does — a mall might run "first hour free," an
airport charges a flat day-rate, a stadium charges per event. Hardcode a formula into `ParkingLot`
and every pricing change becomes a code review of core logic.

A `PricingStrategy` interface with `calculateFee(Ticket, exitTime)` isolates that:
`HourlyRateStrategy`, `FlatRateStrategy`, and `FirstHourFreeStrategy` all implement it, and
`ExitGate` calls whichever one the lot is configured with. Swapping a promotion in becomes a config
change, not a deploy of `ParkingLot`.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: a God ParkingLot class vs decomposed collaborators
slides.markdown:
| | God `ParkingLot` | Decomposed collaborators |
|---|---|---|
| Parking logic | one class owns spot search, pricing, ticketing | `Level` owns spots, `PricingStrategy` owns fees, `Ticket` owns the record |
| Changing pricing | edit the same class that also parks cars | swap a `PricingStrategy` implementation |
| Testability | must stand up the whole lot to test one price formula | test `PricingStrategy` alone with a fake `Ticket` |
| Interview signal | reads as "got it working" | reads as "can extend this live" |

**How to decide:** if the interviewer immediately asks "now add X pricing model" or "now support Y
spot type," that's confirmation they want the decomposed version — build it that way from the
start rather than retrofitting under pressure.

slides.sectionTitle: Compare: reserve exact spot at entry vs reserve type, assign at walk-in
slides.markdown:
| | Reserve exact spot at entry | Reserve type, assign at walk-in |
|---|---|---|
| What the driver gets | a ticket naming spot B2-14 | a ticket naming "a compact spot on level 2" |
| Flexibility | locked even if the driver takes 10 minutes to park | any matching spot works, including one freed in the meantime |
| Multi-entrance lots | two entrances can double-book without cross-entrance locking | each entrance only touches the shared type-bucket, already safe under atomic pop |
| Best fit | small single-entrance lots, valet | large multi-entrance lots (malls, airports) |

**How to decide:** the more entrances and the bigger the lot, the more "reserve type, assign at
walk-in" wins — it needs no cross-entrance coordination and degrades gracefully if a car takes a
while to actually park.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: availability as a boolean scan instead of an index
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "I'll just loop over `level.getSpots()` and return the first one where
`isOccupied() == false`."

**Why it's wrong:** it works in a demo with 20 spots and stops working conceptually at scale —
every park or query becomes O(spots), and there's no natural place to make the reservation atomic,
which is exactly the bug from the concurrency slide.

**Correct model:** maintain the free-spot index (a queue per type) as the source of truth, updated
on park and release. Availability isn't computed by scanning; it's read from a structure that's
always kept current.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: fee from exitTime - entryTime with no rounding rule
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "The fee is just `hourlyRate * (exitTime - entryTime)`, computed in hours."

**Why it's wrong:** a car parked for 61 minutes either gets charged for 2 hours with no stated rule
(feels arbitrary to the driver) or 1.017 hours with no stated rounding (feels arbitrary to the
ticketing system). This exact ambiguity turns into a support-ticket flood in a real product, and an
interviewer watching for edge-case thinking will ask about it directly.

**Correct model:** put the rounding/grace-period rule inside `PricingStrategy` explicitly — e.g.
round up to the next full hour past a 10-minute grace period — so it's a stated policy, not an
accident of the subtraction.

slides.sectionTitle: Extending to EV spots and a multi-lot chain sharing pricing
slides.markdown:
Two follow-ups interviewers reach for. **EV-charging spots**: model as a `ParkingSpot` subtype (or
a `hasCharger` flag) with its own eligibility check inside the assignment strategy — an
EV-assignment strategy filters to charger-equipped spots first, with no change to `ParkingLot` or
`Level`.

**A multi-lot chain** (one company, many physical lots) sharing one pricing policy: lift
`PricingStrategy` out of any single `ParkingLot` instance and inject the same one into each lot's
`ExitGate`. Each lot still owns its own `Level`s and free-spot index independently — only the
pricing decision is shared, exactly the "what changes, what doesn't" question this case study is
built to test.
